system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2161-03-02 18:04:00 to 2161-03-06 17:53:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with type 1 diabetes, depression, and alcohol use disorder, was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) after missing insulin due to alcohol use and poor self-care. She presented with vomiting, polyuria, and polydipsia, with a glucose of 751, pH of 7.04, and anion gap of 37. She was treated with an insulin drip and IV fluids, with resolution of DKA and improvement in acute kidney injury, which was attributed to dehydration. Her insulin regimen was adjusted to 15 units of glargine at bedtime with a sliding scale. Psychiatric evaluation led to enrollment in an outpatient alcohol treatment program due to refusal of inpatient admission. Iron deficiency anemia was addressed with continued supplementation. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans for primary care, mental health, and diabetes management.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ woman with a past medical history 
significant for insulin-dependent diabetes c/b prior episodes of 
DKA who presented with nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, and 
hyperglycemia found to have DKA, likely precipitated by 
abdominal cellulitis/abscess. 
  
# Diabetes Mellitus, Type I, inuslin dependent, poorly 
controlled, complicated
# Diabetic ketoacidosis:  On admission, patient had a metabolic 
acidosis with anion gap of 37 and hyperglycemia with negative 
lactate.  The triggering event appeared to be a skin/soft tissue 
infection of her pannus as well as missed doses of insulin.  She 
denied respiratory or urinary symptoms.  ECG showed no ischemia 
and troponin was negative.  Patient received 4L IVF in the ED 
and was maintained on maintenance fluids.  She was admitted to 
the ICU and was started on an insulin gtt, which was continued 
until her gap was noted to be closed x 2 checks.  She was then 
converted to glargine 15 units + ISS.  Her blood sugars were 
well-controlled on this regimen.  Potassium and other 
electrolytes were monitored and repleted as appropriate.  
    
# Abdominal abscess
# Complicated, purulent cellulitis:  Patient had cellulitis of 
her lower pannus with an area of firm induration with evidence 
of large underlying abscess.  This was likely due to injecting 
insulin with old needles and not maintaining sterile injection 
sites (she was not using alcohol swabs prior to injection).  The 
abscess was I&D'd in the ED and pus was drained.  She was 
started on IV vancomycin and her pain improved.  The wound 
continued to drain significant amounts of pus.  She was 
evaluated by wound care, and ACS. ACS felt she was draining 
satisfactory so did not require further incision/drainage or 
debridement. Repeat US did not reveal additional pockets to 
drain. Given clinical improvement, she was transitioned to 
Bactrim to complete a 5 day course.  She was seen by the wound 
care nurse and was discharged home with ___ to help with 
dressing changes.  She was also seen by the diabetes nurse 
educator, who educated her about clean injection techniques. 
Patient was able to teach back proper sterile tecnnique for 
insulin administration.
    
# Acute Renal Failure:  Cr was 1.4 on admission, likely prerenal 
in the setting of volume depletion secondary to DKA.  This 
normalized with IVF.
   
# Alcohol abuse:  Patient has no history of withdrawal per her 
history.  She has not required benzodiazepines during most 
recent hospital admissions.  She was monitored for signs of 
withdrawal and did not require benzodiazepines.  Home thiamine, 
folate, and MVI were continued.
    
# Normocytic anemia:  On admission, her H/H was higher than her 
most recent baseline which is closer to ___. This was likely 
due to hemoconcentration.  Review of OMR indicates a history of 
low ferritin, consistent with iron-deficiency anemia.  Her H/H 
remained stable and she had no clinical evidence of bleeding or 
hemolysis.
     
# Hypertension:  Lisinopril was held in the setting of ___, but 
this was restarted prior to discharge after kidney function 
normalized.  Home metoprolol was continued. 
    
TRANSITIONAL ISSUES:
=====================
[ ] Please follow-up on patient's blood sugars and adjust 
insulin regimen as needed.
[ ] Continue to encourage patient to use clean/new needles and 
appropriate technique when injecting insulin in order to help 
prevent abdominal abscesses from forming.

# Diabetic ketoacidosis:  On admission, patient had a metabolic 
acidosis with anion gap of 37 and hyperglycemia with negative 
lactate.  The triggering event appeared to be a skin/soft tissue 
infection of her pannus as well as missed doses of insulin.  She 
denied respiratory or urinary symptoms.  ECG showed no ischemia 
and troponin was negative.  Patient received 4L IVF in the ED 
and was maintained on maintenance fluids.  She was admitted to 
the ICU and was started on an insulin gtt, which was continued 
until her gap was noted to be closed x 2 checks.  She was then 
converted to glargine 15 units + ISS.  Her blood sugars were 
well-controlled on this regimen.  Potassium and other 
electrolytes were monitored and repleted as appropriate.  
    
# Abdominal abscess
# Complicated, purulent cellulitis:  Patient had cellulitis of 
her lower pannus with an area of firm induration with evidence 
of large underlying abscess.  This was likely due to injecting 
insulin with old needles and not maintaining sterile injection 
sites (she was not using alcohol swabs prior to injection).  The 
abscess was I&D'd in the ED and pus was drained.  She was 
started on IV vancomycin and her pain improved.  The wound 
continued to drain significant amounts of pus.  She was 
evaluated by wound care, and ACS. ACS felt she was draining 
satisfactory so did not require further incision/drainage or 
debridement. Repeat US did not reveal additional pockets to 
drain. Given clinical improvement, she was transitioned to 
Bactrim to complete a 5 day course.  She was seen by the wound 
care nurse and was discharged home with ___ to help with 
dressing changes.  She was also seen by the diabetes nurse 
educator, who educated her about clean injection techniques. 
Patient was able to teach back proper sterile tecnnique for 
insulin administration.
    
# Acute Renal Failure:  Cr was 1.4 on admission, likely prerenal 
in the setting of volume depletion secondary to DKA.  This 
normalized with IVF.
   
# Alcohol abuse:  Patient has no history of withdrawal per her 
history.  She has not required benzodiazepines during most 
recent hospital admissions.  She was monitored for signs of 
withdrawal and did not require benzodiazepines.  Home thiamine, 
folate, and MVI were continued.
    
# Normocytic anemia:  On admission, her H/H was higher than her 
most recent baseline which is closer to ___. This was likely 
due to hemoconcentration.  Review of OMR indicates a history of 
low ferritin, consistent with iron-deficiency anemia.  Her H/H 
remained stable and she had no clinical evidence of bleeding or 
hemolysis.
     
# Hypertension:  Lisinopril was held in the setting of ___, but 
this was restarted prior to discharge after kidney function 
normalized.  Home metoprolol was continued. 
    
TRANSITIONAL ISSUES:
=====================
[ ] Please follow-up on patient's blood sugars and adjust 
insulin regimen as needed.
[ ] Continue to encourage patient to use clean/new needles and 
appropriate technique when injecting insulin in order to help 
prevent abdominal abscesses from forming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU now. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really sick—nauseous, throwing up, and my blood sugar was through the roof. I had this abscess on my belly, and after a hot shower it started draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You also had very high glucose—731—and signs of diabetic ketoacidosis. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s bad, right? I skipped my Lantus last night because I felt so off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That likely contributed. The infection on your abdomen also stressed your body. We drained the abscess in the ER, and you’re on antibiotics now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it was that serious. I just thought it was a pimple.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common with insulin injections if the site isn’t clean. We’ll talk more about safe injection practices later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach still feels weird, but I’m not vomiting anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your labs show your kidneys were stressed—creatinine was 1.4—but that’s improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s likely from dehydration due to DKA. It should return to normal, which it’s already starting to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. My sugars have been so hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your insulin drip closely. Once your acid levels normalize, we’ll switch you to injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the same needle a few times… is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that increases infection risk. We’ll have the diabetes educator show you safer techniques.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work is improving. Anion gap is closing, and your pH is rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll transition you off the insulin drip today and restart your glargine at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 15 units. Should I go back to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll monitor your sugars and adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My belly incision is still draining a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The wound care team checked it—drainage is good, no need for more surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said something about a culture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they found Group B Strep and some Candida in the wound. That’s why you’re on vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not uncommon in skin infections. We’re treating it, and you’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been trying to eat, but not much stays down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on light foods. Small, frequent meals might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look great. Glucose is 120, bicarbonate is 18, and anion gap is nearly closed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Getting there. We’ll keep you on IV antibiotics a bit longer, then switch to oral Bactrim.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably a couple more days. We want to make sure your sugars stay stable and the wound keeps improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The diabetes nurse came by yesterday. I learned a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. She said you taught back the technique perfectly—clean swabs, rotating sites, new needles each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize how much I was cutting corners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It happens. The key is consistency. We also restarted your lisinopril—kidney function is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about my blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. We’ll keep monitoring. Your hemoglobin dropped a bit, but it’s likely from the infection, not bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your ultrasound shows no new fluid pockets. The area is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more procedures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The drainage is sufficient. We’ll send you home with a nurse to help with dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Bactrim for five days. And we’re adjusting your insulin—12 units at breakfast and 12 at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To better match your body’s needs. We’ll fine-tune it at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll stick to it this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Your mental health and alcohol use are also important—we can connect you with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking less. Maybe I should talk to someone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up. For now, focus on healing. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are normal. You’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue all your meds, especially insulin. Use new needles, clean sites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And the visiting nurse will come?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily for dressing changes. Call us if the wound gets red, swollen, or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary doctor in a week and the diabetes clinic soon after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with type 1 diabetes, depression, and alcohol use disorder, was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by an abdominal abscess and missed insulin doses. She presented with nausea, vomiting, and severe hyperglycemia. In the ED, she received IV fluids, insulin, and antibiotics, and underwent incision and drainage of the abscess. Her DKA resolved with treatment, and renal function normalized. The wound showed clinical improvement with adequate drainage, and she was transitioned to oral antibiotics. A diabetes educator reinforced proper injection techniques, which the patient demonstrated correctly. She was discharged home with a visiting nurse for wound care, adjusted insulin regimen, and follow-up plans for primary care and diabetes management.
